IMPORTANT: The text inside "keystrokes" will be used completely verbatim as keystrokes. Write commands exactly as you want them sent to the terminal:

The "duration" attribute specifies the number of seconds to wait for the command to complete (default: 1.0) before the next command will be executed. On immediate tasks (e.g., cd, ls, echo, cat) set a duration of 0.1 seconds. On commands (e.g., gcc, find, rustc) set a duration of 1.0 seconds. On slow commands (e.g., make, python3 [long running script], wget [file]) set an appropriate duration as you determine necessary.

It is better to set a smaller duration than a longer duration. It is always possible to wait again if the prior output has not finished, by running {"keystrokes": "", "duration": 10.0} on subsequent requests to wait longer. Never wait longer than 60 seconds; prefer to poll to see intermediate result status.

Important notes:
- Each command's keystrokes are sent exactly as written to the terminal
- Do not include extra whitespace before or after the keystrokes unless it's part of the intended command
- Extra text before or after the JSON will generate warnings but be tolerated
- The JSON must be valid - use proper escaping for quotes and special characters within strings
- Commands array can be empty if you want to wait without taking action

"""Simple log parsing utilities for logkit."""


def parse_log(path):
    """Parse a log file into a list of entries.

    Each line is expected in the form:
        TIMESTAMP LEVEL MESSAGE...
    """
    entries = []
    with open(path) as f:
        for line in f:
            line = line.rstrip("\n")
            timestamp, level, message = line.split(" ", 2)
            entries.append(
                {"timestamp": timestamp, "level": level, "message": message}
            )
    return entries

from pathlib import Path

from logkit.parser import parse_log


def _write(tmp_path, name, content):
    p = tmp_path / name
    p.write_text(content)
    return p


def test_parses_standard_lines(tmp_path):
    p = _write(
        tmp_path,
        "a.log",
        "2024-01-01T00:00:00 INFO server started\n"
        "2024-01-01T00:00:01 WARN disk low\n",
    )
    entries = parse_log(p)
    assert entries == [
        {"timestamp": "2024-01-01T00:00:00", "level": "INFO", "message": "server started"},
        {"timestamp": "2024-01-01T00:00:01", "level": "WARN", "message": "disk low"},
    ]


def test_handles_blank_lines(tmp_path):
    p = _write(
        tmp_path,
        "b.log",
        "2024-01-01T00:00:00 INFO server started\n"
        "\n"
        "2024-01-01T00:00:01 WARN disk low\n",
    )
    entries = parse_log(p)
    assert entries == [
        {"timestamp": "2024-01-01T00:00:00", "level": "INFO", "message": "server started"},
        {"timestamp": "2024-01-01T00:00:01", "level": "WARN", "message": "disk low"},
    ]

steps.message:
Analysis: The parser currently strips only the trailing newline and immediately splits every line into three fields. A truly blank line becomes an empty string, so line.split(" ", 2) returns too few values and raises ValueError. The tests include a blank-line case and expect it to be ignored.
Plan: Modify logkit/parser.py to continue the loop when a line is blank or whitespace-only, then run pytest to verify the full test suite passes.

def parse_log(path):
